vignette:
The Weight of What He Saw

Minh is a 74-year-old Vietnamese man who has lived in the United States for nearly four decades, long enough that his English carries only a faint trace of the accent his grandchildren find charming. He spent the better part of his adult life working as a welder, and even now, two years into a retirement his wife insisted upon, he keeps a small workshop in the garage where he tinkers with metal scraps - bending, cutting, joining things together. It is, he says quietly, the only time his hands feel useful.

He was seventeen years old when the war came fully to his village in the Mekong Delta. He does not speak of it easily, and when he does, he tends to look at a fixed point somewhere past the room, as though the memory lives just beyond the wall. In the spring of 1968, during a period of intense fighting, he witnessed the deaths of his younger brother and two neighbors when their hamlet was caught in crossfire. He spent nearly three days hiding in a drainage canal, submerged to his chin in water and mud, listening to sounds he has never been able to name adequately in either Vietnamese or English. He was eventually found by relatives and survived, but something fundamental shifted in him during those seventy-odd hours in the dark water, and it has never fully shifted back.

He immigrated in the mid-1980s, married, raised three children, and built a life that, from the outside, looked whole. His wife, Lan, describes him as a devoted father and a hard worker - a man who poured himself into the physical demands of welding with what she now recognizes as a kind of desperate purpose. The noise of the shop floor, the brightness of the arc, the heat - he tolerated all of it without complaint. What he could not tolerate was silence, or darkness, or the sound of distant fireworks, which his neighbors still set off every Fourth of July and which send him into the back bedroom with the television turned loud.

Since retiring, the structure that kept certain things at bay has loosened. He sleeps poorly, waking between two and four in the morning with his heart pounding and his undershirt soaked through. The dreams are not always the same, but they return to the same place - the canal, the smell of the water, the sounds. During the day he finds himself startled by ordinary things: a car backfiring, a door slamming, the neighbor's dog. He describes a persistent feeling of being on guard, of scanning, though he cannot always say what he is scanning for. He has become irritable in ways that confuse and hurt Lan, who has noticed that he flinches when she approaches him from behind.

He rarely speaks of the war to his children. He carries a belief, rooted in both temperament and culture, that suffering is something a man manages privately, that to burden others with it is a form of weakness or selfishness. When his youngest daughter finally persuaded him to speak with a psychologist - framing it, cleverly, as something that might help him sleep - he agreed with visible reluctance.

In session, he is courteous and precise. He chooses his words carefully, sometimes pausing for long stretches. He has mentioned, more than once, that he does not fully understand why these things are happening to him now, after so many years. He built a life. He welded things together. He thought the past had been managed.

What strikes the clinician most is not the severity of what he describes, but the exhaustion behind it - the exhaustion of a man who has spent more than fifty years holding something at arm's length, and whose arms are finally, quietly, giving out.
